title: EFC — A Deep Dive into the Halo Concept
description: Conceptual overview of the halo in cosmology, emphasizing its role as a stabilizer and regulator of energy and mass flow around galaxies and clusters. Synthesizes evidence from rotation curves, gravitational lensing, X-ray intracluster emissions, and simulations to motivate halos as dynamic, dark-matter-dominated envelopes that preserve structure and large-scale symmetry within the Energy-Flow Cosmology framing.

key_results.main_finding: Argues that dark-matter-dominated halos act as dynamic regulators and stabilizers of galactic and cluster-scale energy and mass flows, consistent with rotation curves, lensing, and ICM X-ray observations.
datasets_used: X-ray observations of the intracluster medium
Numerical simulations of galaxy and cluster formation

kill_criteria: KC1: High-precision weak+strong lensing mass maps for a representative sample of spiral galaxies and clusters show mass profiles that truncate at or within the luminous radius, with no extended halo component (e.g., NFW-like) at >95% confidence.

KC2: Spatially resolved HI/stellar rotation curves extending to >10 exponential scale lengths are simultaneously fit by baryonic mass models without any dark halo across a broad population of galaxies.

KC3: Deep X-ray and Sunyaev–Zel'dovich measurements of cluster ICM temperature and pressure profiles require no additional gravitating mass beyond baryons (i.e., are inconsistent with confinement by extended halos).

KC4: Cosmological simulations omitting dark matter halos (or any extended mass component) successfully and simultaneously reproduce observed galaxy stability, satellite kinematics, and lensing statistics.
KC5: Large-scale structure and CMB anisotropy analyses find that models without extended halos provide equal or better fits to observations across multiple probes without fine-tuning.
